History:
- Presenting complaint: Several months (≈2 months) of increasing anxiety focused on mornings/leaving the house and work-related situations with associated palpitations and insomnia.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began ~2 months ago, coinciding with starting a new, stressful job; gradual worsening with increased daily morning dread and cumulative impact on sleep and activities.
- Context/triggers/timing: Worry is predominantly triggered by work, interactions with a difficult boss, and commuting (public transport). Symptoms are worst in the morning on waking and pre-work; palpitations occur on waking and at times during the day.
- Associated symptoms: Racing, irregular palpitations lasting minutes up to ~10 minutes; marked difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep (est. 3–4 hours, shallow), early-morning panic, daytime fatigue, reduced enjoyment/interest in hobbies (running, tennis), social avoidance, low mood. No suicidal ideation.
- Previous episodes/interventions: No prior similar episodes; has not sought therapy previously but is willing to try one-to-one/talking therapy. Mother has history of depression.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: None documented in transcript.
- Surgical/hospitalizations: Not recorded.
- Allergies: Not recorded.
- Medications: No regular medications documented.
- Family history: Mother with past depression (patient-reported).
- Social history: Lives with parents. Alcohol: drinks socially with heavier intake on weekends (no quantified amounts recorded). Occasional smoking. No recreational drug use reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals/physical exam: Not recorded.
- Reported/observed findings: Intermittent irregular, rapid palpitations (patient-perceived), no sustained chest pain (patient reports discomfort when heart racing but denies classic chest pain), shallow sleep, reduced energy, tearfulness/low mood. No syncope reported.
- Relevant negatives: No suicidal ideation; no prior hospital admissions for cardiac issues; no reported recreational drug use. Physical exam and vital signs not performed/documented.

Impression:
- Primary clinical impression: Work-related anxiety most consistent with an adjustment disorder presenting with prominent anxiety, insomnia, and anxiety-associated palpitations.
- Other plausible diagnoses consistent with the transcript:
  - Generalized anxiety disorder — features of excessive worry, insomnia and functional impairment are present but duration (~2 months) is below the 6-month threshold for formal GAD diagnosis.
  - Paroxysmal cardiac arrhythmia (e.g., SVT/AF) — irregular, brief palpitations described; cannot be excluded without rhythm assessment.
- (No conflict noted between transcript and DDx; DDx supports and expands differential consistent with the transcript.)

Management Plan:
- Immediate/advised actions:
  - Patient advised to self-refer to NHS talking therapy (IAPT) / one-to-one therapy; clinician to send referral link/resources (patient agreed).
  - Arrange basic blood tests to exclude reversible triggers for palpitations/anxiety (tests not specified in transcript); patient instructed to call support line to arrange tests.
  - GP follow-up planned approximately one week after blood tests to review results and reassess symptoms.
  - Provide online self-help resources and brief sleep hygiene advice (clinician to add details to notes).
  - Pharmacotherapy not recommended as first-line at this stage; to consider if symptoms persist/worsen (per clinician discussion).
  - Safety netting: patient advised to contact GP/return if anxiety worsens to the point of being unable to cope with work/daily activities.
- Immediate medications/interventions given during consult: None documented.

Patient Summary:
- Valerie Cole, ~2 months of escalating work-related anxiety after starting a new stressful job, causing morning panic, irregular palpitations, poor sleep (≈3–4 hours), low mood and reduced functioning. Likely adjustment disorder with anxiety; plan is talking therapy/self-help, basic blood tests to exclude physiologic causes, and GP follow-up after tests.

Key Takeaways:
- Self-refer to NHS talking therapy (IAPT) — clinician will send link/resources.
- Arrange basic blood tests via the support line to exclude medical causes of palpitations; follow-up with GP about results.
- Contact GP/return promptly if symptoms worsen or if unable to cope with work/daily tasks.

Next Steps:
- Patient to call support line to arrange the basic blood tests (tests not specified in transcript).
- Primary care follow-up arranged ~1 week after blood tests to review results and progress.
- Patient to self-refer for talking therapy and begin online resources while awaiting therapy.
- Reassess need for pharmacologic therapy if no improvement or worsening of symptoms.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs, physical examination findings, medications list and doses, documented allergies, specific blood tests ordered, ECG/ambulatory cardiac monitoring (not requested in transcript), quantified alcohol intake.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted — DDx recommendations (arrhythmia, thyroid, substance causes) are listed in reasoning and the clinician recommended basic blood tests; no DDx item directly contradicted the transcript. 
- Transcript quality: Consultation transcript is clear and complete for history; no significant inaudible segments.
